blocks.prompt: The Tiger With Stripes on Its Skin
blocks.text: A tiger is the biggest cat in the world. It is bigger than a lion. A tiger has orange fur with black stripes. The stripes help it hide. In tall grass, the stripes look like shadows. A tiger hunts by itself. It creeps up slow and low. Its paws have soft pads, so it makes no sound. Then it jumps. Most tigers live in forests in Asia. Baby tigers are called cubs. A cub stays with its mom for about two years. She teaches it how to hunt.

blocks.prompt: The Cat That Hunts Alone
blocks.text: Lions live in groups called prides. Tigers do not. A tiger lives alone, walks alone, and hunts alone. The only tigers that share a home are a mother and her cubs. A tiger is built for one thing: getting close without being noticed. Its orange coat with black stripes looks bright to you, but a deer cannot see the color orange the way you can. To a deer, a tiger in tall grass looks like grass. The tiger's paws have thick pads, so it moves in silence. It creeps closer and closer, sometimes for an hour, until it is only a few steps away. Then it explodes forward. Even so, the tiger usually fails. Deer are fast and they listen well. Only about one hunt in ten ends with a meal. A tiger may go days without eating, then eat a huge amount at once. The strangest fact is this. If you shaved a tiger, it would still have stripes. The pattern is in its skin, not just its fur.

blocks.prompt: Hidden in Plain Orange
blocks.text: Here is a puzzle. The tiger is an ambush hunter. Everything about it is built for going unseen: silent pads on its feet, patience that can last an hour, a body that can cross a wide gap in one leap. And then it wears bright orange. The answer is that the tiger is not hiding from you. It is hiding from deer and wild pigs, and their eyes are not built like yours. You have three kinds of color sensors in your eyes. A deer has two. It cannot tell orange from green. To a deer, a tiger creeping through tall grass is a gray-green smudge broken up by black bars. The stripes finish the trick. They cut the outline of a huge cat into pieces, so the deer's brain never assembles a tiger out of them. Scientists call this disruptive coloration. The stripes do a second job. No two tigers wear the same pattern, the way no two people share a fingerprint. Researchers hide cameras along forest trails and count individual tigers by their stripes, and that is how we know how few are left. Those stripes are not only fur. The pattern is printed into the tiger's skin as well. Shave one, and the design is still there.

blocks.prompt: The Cat That Is Losing Its Ground
blocks.text: A tiger is a contradiction that works. It is the largest cat alive, and an Amur tiger from the forests of the Russian Far East can pass six hundred pounds. It is also, when it wants to be, invisible. The invisibility is not luck. It is arithmetic. Your eyes carry three kinds of color sensor. A deer carries two, and without the third it cannot separate orange from green. The tiger's coat, so loud to you, dissolves into the grass for the animal that matters. The black bars finish the job by breaking the cat's outline into fragments, a trick biologists call disruptive coloration. Add pads that silence a four-hundred-pound footfall and the patience to close a hundred paces over an hour, and you have an ambush that works about one time in ten. That failure rate is not a flaw. It is the price of hunting animals that are faster than you. Almost everything about the tiger is solitary. Lions cooperate; tigers do not. An adult tiger holds a territory and patrols it alone, marking the edges with scent and clawed trees. In the Russian Far East, where prey is thin, a single male may claim more than four hundred square miles. The only lasting company a tiger keeps is a mother with her cubs, and even that ends after about two years, when she drives them off to find ground of their own. Which brings us to the trouble. A solitary animal that needs hundreds of square miles of forest, and a full-grown deer every week or so, needs one thing above all: space. Space is what has been taken. Tigers once ranged from Turkey to the eastern coast of Russia and south to Bali. Three kinds are already gone forever. Today wild tigers occupy roughly five percent of the land they once held, and they number somewhere near five thousand five hundred. Here is the fact that should stop you. There are thousands of tigers living in cages, back yards, and roadside attractions in the United States alone, a captive population that rivals the number walking free in the whole world. The species is not rare because it failed. It is rare because we took the ground it was standing on.

meta.templateLabel: The Tiger With Stripes on Its Skin

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Panthera tigris, the largest living cat
Hind legs longer than front legs, loaded like a spring
Deer are dichromats: no sensor for red or orange
Disruptive coloration slices up the outline
Stripes are printed into the skin, not just the fur
Three tiger populations are already extinct

blocks.prompt: The Ambush and the Arithmetic
blocks.text: Start with the contradiction, because everything interesting about the tiger lives inside it. Here is an animal built entirely for concealment. Its feet are padded so that four hundred pounds of cat can cross dry leaves without a sound. It will hold a crouch for an hour to gain twenty paces. Its hind legs are longer than its front legs, loading the body like a spring. And it carries all of this equipment while wearing bright orange. The contradiction dissolves the moment you stop asking who the tiger is hiding from. It is not hiding from us. Human eyes carry three kinds of color sensor; a deer's eyes carry two, and the missing one is the one that reads red and orange. A deer looking at a tiger in dry grass is not looking at orange at all. It is looking at a dull green-gray shape, and the black bars are already at work on that shape, slicing the outline of an enormous predator into disconnected fragments that the deer's brain never bothers to assemble. Biologists call the technique disruptive coloration. The tiger is not badly camouflaged. It is camouflaged for the correct audience. The stripes carry a second signature that the tiger never intended. No two tigers wear the same pattern. Field researchers string camera traps along forest paths and identify individuals by their bars, the way a detective works a fingerprint, and it is precisely this method that gives us our census. The pattern also runs deeper than fur: it is printed into the skin underneath, so a shaved tiger is still a striped tiger. Now the arithmetic, which is less charming. All that engineering produces a hunt that succeeds roughly one time in ten. A tiger is not a machine that catches deer; it is a machine that fails nine times and survives anyway, because the tenth attempt feeds it for days. To run those odds, a tiger needs prey in quantity, and to hold prey in quantity it needs land. An adult patrols alone, marking boundaries with scent and clawed trunks, tolerating no rival. In the Russian Far East, where deer are scarce, one male's territory can exceed four hundred square miles. That number is the whole conservation problem stated in one line. You cannot keep a solitary animal that requires four hundred square miles by protecting a park of forty. Tigers once ran from eastern Turkey to the Pacific coast of Russia and south through the islands to Bali. Three of those populations, the Caspian, the Javan, and the Bali tigers, are gone and are not coming back. What remains occupies roughly five percent of that old map, and the whole wild species now numbers around five thousand five hundred animals, fewer than the people in a small town. There is a tempting way to feel better about this. Tigers breed readily in captivity; thousands live in zoos, private compounds, and roadside attractions, and in the United States alone the captive population rivals the wild one worldwide. But a tiger in a cage is not doing any of the things described above. It is not holding a territory, not running the ten-to-one odds, not keeping deer numbers in check across a forest. It is a tiger-shaped animal in a box. The species is not endangered because its design failed. Every part of the design still works. It is endangered because the design requires room, and room is the one thing we have not been willing to leave it.
